source-ref: Alan ruling 2026-06-24, held dark until the first death

content.rule: THE LOOP: dying returns Alan to the floor-1 entrance, staged exactly as the very first scene was, and that symmetry is the reveal. RETAINED across a death: all memory; character level, attributes, skills, titles, affinities and class progress; the HP, Focus and Stamina maxes. LOST: equipment, consumables and anything carried, which belonged to that run of the world. Companions reset and do not remember him; he remembers them. The tower regenerates with enemies respawned and the layout shifted enough that memorisation alone is not the answer, and the upper floors scale, so retained power plus foreknowledge is a real head start rather than a stroll.
content.implications: Alan does not know the loop exists until he dies. Zero foreshadowing: no winks, no asking whether he is sure, no save-point language, and the first death plays completely straight, because for all he knows in the moment he lost. Every design settled from now must stay consistent with the loop so that the reveal contradicts nothing already said. The game master does not engineer a death; play decides when it comes, and the reveal waits as long as it waits. Once the loop is understood it becomes a tool: die to reset, climb again faster and stronger, and push higher than before. The companion reset is revisitable once companions exist and the loop is out.

source-ref: Alan ruling 2026-06-24, the whole-tower escalation mandate

content.rule: THE TOWER ESCALATES. Every floor is measured on two counts and should advance on both, and may regress on neither. NOVELTY: each floor opens a tactical demand no earlier floor made — the first was a chokepoint, then water, then acoustics, then dark and height and timing, then trust and verification. MAGNITUDE: later floors are genuinely bigger and harder rather than only different — more rooms and more interacting systems; a mechanic that evolves across the floor rather than one static gimmick; a threat shape that varies from a single warden to a coordinated pair to a staged multi-phase boss; and lethality that grows with the player's own power, so a later boss carries a real risk of killing rather than a longer bar.
content.implications: The seductive default is scout, then light or solve, then one boss undone by its readable weakness. That was right for the first four floors and is to be broken deliberately from the fifth: multi-phase bosses, puzzles of identification rather than placement, encounters with more than one threat, climaxes carried by the floor itself, staged objectives. Reading beating brute force stays the spine; the shape around it keeps changing. Every floor's lethality is calibrated against the player's sheet as it stands when the floor is written, and every escalation is verified against the mechanics rather than asserted in prose. Each floor leaves the next a clear step: what demand is still unused, and where the size should go.

source-ref: ratified tower-wide 2026-06-24, from the floor-5 ruling

content.rule: A kill of a true form is permanent. A retreat from an enemy only wounded returns that enemy to full when the player comes back. Permanence is counted per enemy rather than per floor: a floor of three wardens where one is killed and the player flees keeps that one dead and returns the other two. What the player keeps across a retreat is everything learned — the tells, the reads, the layout — and what the player loses is the damage dealt to anything not finished.
content.implications: This closes the grind of chipping an enemy down across rests, and makes a floor's real gate whether a true form can be killed in one sustained push. The asymmetry is what makes it read as fair rather than punishing: it rewards the push and the learning and denies only the attrition. The fiction of the recovery varies by floor. An illusion or a construct re-weaves to pristine at once, owing nothing to how long the player was gone. Something physical or living recovers by resting, and the heal has to be carried by time genuinely passing: a breather at the threshold is a partial recovery at most, and only a long rest is a full one. On a physical floor the player's own recovery and the enemy's run off one clock, so the player cannot buy a full restore without granting the enemy the same, and half-resting buys neither. An illusion floor decouples this deliberately, which is why its reset feels eerie where the physical one feels fair. The rule and the per-enemy permanence are fixed tower-wide; the flavour of a recovery and the guardrail on a physical reset may be amended for a floor whose fiction needs it, noted where that floor is written.

source-ref: settled 2026-06-24 from the floor files, before affinities were first played

content.rule: Every drop flagged an essence seed carries latent essence of one element, settled before play from the floor files. Floor one: the Ashling's cooling cinder is ember. Floor two: the Drowned Sentry's fire-purged iron rivet is ember again in its forge cast, and the Glut's swarm-ichor sac is alchemy. Floor three: the Hollow Cantor's tuning-shard of folded sound is sound, and the cracked focus-crystal in the gallery alcove is mind. Floor four: the Gloomward Stalker's eye-lens is dark, and the Counterweight Colossus's winding-drum core is force. Essence deeper in the tower resists harder: the resistance an absorption is held against runs about fifty on floor one, fifty-two on floor two, fifty-five on floor three and fifty-eight on floor four. Not every drop is a seed. The floor-three keystone, the Warden's stone gauntlet, the Colossus's chain-length, the Sentry's pauldron and the Stalker's hide carry no essence at all and feed crafting only. The drum core is both a force seed and the heaviest crafting core yet.
content.implications: Ember has two seeds across the first four floors by design, because a second seed of an element already held is the cheapest way to climb it: the absorption mechanic trains an absorber six for holding the element against three for holding anything else. The other five elements appear once each, and their second seeds wait on floors from the fifth up. A dual-use drop is a real choice between feeding an affinity and feeding the forge, and the game master presents it as one rather than settling it. A seed is consumed by the absorption whatever the band, so no seed grants twice. A re-climb after a death re-seeds the drops while the affinity already banked persists, so absorbing again is for a new element or for topping one rather than for stacking the same element without end. An unabsorbed seed is lost on a death where a banked affinity is kept, which makes absorbing before risking a death the safe play; that stays held dark until the loop is understood.

source-ref: the seam settled 2026-06-24 alongside the affinity spec, deliberately not built

content.rule: Crafting is the axis that opens beside affinities higher in the tower, and affinities are its essence input. What is settled here is the seam and not the system. An affinity at manipulation or above can imbue a weapon or an item with its element, so the thing carries the element rather than the wielder: an ember imbue on the iron bar makes its strikes carry heat and match a heat weakness innately. An imbue costs an absorption act and focus. At the first tier an emerged essence skill already approximates this for a moment, and imbuing is what makes it persist on the item. A recipe consumes an affinity tier, essence as either a banked cost or a held seed of the element, and a material core, and answers an imbued or a crafted item. The cores are the keystone, the gauntlet, the chain-length, the drum core and their like.
content.implications: This is a seam rather than a build: no code runs crafting and none should until the tower reaches the floors where it opens. What the seam buys now is that nothing already settled forecloses it. Seeds are typed, cores are named and held apart from seeds, and a dual-use drop already exists in play. When crafting is built it reads the affinity tier and the element table and needs nothing new from either.

source-ref: locked 2026-06-24, the three skills emerged in play

content.rule: Three skills have emerged in play and climb the same seven rungs. EMBER CHANNEL conducts his own ember into a held weapon: self-sourced, transient, fixed to the element. EMBER BURST releases it all at once as an outward pulse into a zone, the area counterpart to the channel, and its axis up the ladder is aim, metering and where the pulse is placed. ESSENCE INFUSION is a different kind: it extracts an essence from a raw source and binds it into a separate object, so it is external-sourced, persistent and element-neutral. Being a motor technique rather than an element, infusion has no matched affinity and takes no affinity bias, which is why the cold-ichor imbue took none, the element being wrong for his ember. It still adds by its rung like any skill. Its axis is binding quality: whether the bind holds under pressure, how long it lasts before it bleeds off, and what the focus costs. Binding an essence of the pole opposite the binder's own costs more and binds shakier, and that tax shrinks each rung: heavy at novice, noticeable at journeyman, merely costlier at master, and immaterial at sage.
content.implications: A skill's rung is judged against the general ladder, and what a skill's own entry adds is only its axis, meaning what improving at THIS skill improves. Where the ladder says a journeyman does it when they set themselves to it, for the burst that is a metered pulse onto a lured or massed target from stable ground, and for infusion it is a stable bind made with the source in hand and time to work. Applying a skill to something it was not drilled for, or fusing it with footwork or another essence, reads as a strong expert and is the natural sign of reaching toward grandmaster. Integration is a grading signal rather than a rung of its own: the seven rung names are locked and there is no eighth. The live placement of every skill is the character sheet and nothing else.
